newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Metals lead a commodity rally.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Metals lead a commodity rally.

text.p: The price of nickel jumped on Monday to a 9-1/2 month high after workers at Russia's giant Arctic metals complex at Norilsk moved closer to a strike over pay and holiday arrears.
Other industrial metals were also rallying with zinc close to its best for 4-1/2 years. And labour unrest among Brazilian portworkers fuelled sharp rallies in coffee, soybeans and wheat.

Workers at Norilsk said on Monday they had adopted a strike plan to take effect if demands were not met within 10 days. But management at the plant, which supplies platinum and palladium as well as nickel, said it could not afford their claims.

Nickel for three-months delivery on the London Metal Exchange (LME) reached the highest since last May at $8,320 per tonne. The metal is in demand for making stainless steel and stocks are low, so that the economic impact may soon be felt.
In Duesselorf, the German steel trade association Edelstahl handels vereinigung (EHV) said high nickel prices are likely to bring rising surcharges in the German stainless steel sector.
"A slight increase in March should be followed by another, more sizeable, surcharge in April," EHV said. "Stockholders should consider these developments when planning future business decisions."
Platinum and palladium were slightly easier from last week's values on profit-taking after they had made brisk gains, fuelled by the Norilsk troubles, in February.
The month saw palladium rise 25 percent and platinum 17 percent. Dealers said that a Norilsk strike had now been factored in to these prices.

Russia is the biggest producer of palladium and the second largest after South Africa of platinum, mainly used in electronics and auto catalysts to clean up exhaust fumes. Japan is by far the largest consumer.
Gold traded firmer on Monday after a late Friday rally in New York on fund short covering. It fixed in London at $362.15 per ounce, up from $358.60 on Friday.
Zinc, copper and aluminium were among base metals to extend rallies. Traders said the advance on these was helped by the way that nickel aroused speculative interest.
Aluminium touched a high at $1,691 per tonne, its best for a year, in a market underpinned by good consumer demand and positive technical charts.
Zinc was at its strongest for almost 4-1/2 years on speculative buying and low stocks at $1,240 per tonne. Copper ended in London above $2,400 per tonne.
World oil prices traded at their lowest since last August, sinking to around $18.75 for a barrel of the benchmark North Sea Brent Blend crude.
Oil extended a 20 percent slide from just below $25 in January on views that the market is well supplied and the peak of northern hemisphere winter fuel demand is over.
"Overall both European and US fundamentals are still fairly weak," said Leslie Nicholas, analyst at GNI Ltd in London.

Coffee prices, which have advanced by 50 percent so far this year, were again strong -- this time because of a pay dispute at Brazil's port of Paranagua and union threats to strike at other ports in that country.

Benchmark London robusta coffee futures for May touched $1,655 per tonne, within sight of the February peak in the current cycle which was at $1,705. New York Arabica May futures hit new contract highs at 182 cents per pound.
Strength in coffee is also underpinned by low consumer stocks against a backdrop of concerns that supply from Latin America may fall short of expectations.

The labour unrest in the port sector in Brazil, a major grower of soybeans, also lifted futures for that commodity on the Chicago Board of Trade with the May contract gaining more than 10 cents a bushel to trade above $8.00.
Wheat and corn (maize) were dragged in to the rally in Chicago.
